claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by low-temperature annealing refines the grain structure of magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Severe plastic deformation followed by low-temperature annealing increases the coercive field of magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Standard-cast magnetic high-entropy alloys have relatively coarse grains.
Standard-cast magnetic high-entropy alloys exhibit conventional microstructural disorder.
The treatment is intended to retain a fine-grained microstructure while consolidating the sample.
The proposed effect is expected in a magnetic Fe-Co-Ni-based high-entropy alloy measured at room temperature.
The processing should produce grain sizes in the nanometer-to-sub-micrometer regime without inducing superparamagnetism.
Grain refinement increases the density of grain boundaries and associated defects.
Grain boundaries and associated defects act as effective pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Reducing grain size increases the number and effectiveness of domain-wall pinning sites.
Enhanced pinning restricts magnetic domain-wall motion.
Restricting domain-wall motion raises the applied magnetic field required to reverse magnetization.
The treated material will have a higher coercive field than a matched standard-cast baseline.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on the degree of grain refinement.
The coercivity increase should hold only while grain size remains in a regime that enhances domain-wall pinning without superparamagnetic effects dominating.
The relevant grain-size regime is typically tens to hundreds of nanometers.
The quantitative coercivity increase and optimal processing parameters may vary with composition and processing conditions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase, despite confirmed grain refinement, would falsify the hypothesis.
